title: Daily Life Rules That Get Students in Trouble
summary: Some of these rules are manners. Some carry criminal penalties. Guides blur the two, and the official guidebook does not — the line is worth knowing exactly.
body_html:
Advice about living in Japan arrives as an undifferentiated list: sort your rubbish, be quiet at night, don't talk on the train. All presented with the same weight, as if they were all etiquette.

They are not. Some of these carry criminal penalties and some are mildly annoying to your neighbours. The official guidebook distinguishes them clearly, and knowing which is which is more useful than memorising the whole list.

The ones with penalties attached

Three items in the guidebook come with legal consequences stated.

Dumping rubbish outside designated places. You must not carelessly dispose of rubbish anywhere other than the places designated, and if you do, a criminal penalty may be imposed. [source:1] Not a fine from the building manager — a criminal penalty.

Littering. Many municipalities have ordinances prohibiting the discarding of empty cans and cigarette butts on the roadside, and administrative or criminal penalties may be imposed. [source:1]

Operating a phone while driving or cycling. Operating a mobile phone while driving a car or riding a bicycle is prohibited by law. [source:1] Note the bicycle. This catches students more than any other rule in the chapter, because a bicycle does not feel like driving.

Separately, the guidebook advises against operating a phone while walking, on the grounds that you may injure a passer-by or yourself. [source:1] That one is advice, not law — and the difference is exactly the distinction worth carrying.

The ones that are manners

The guidebook is explicit that these are manner violations rather than offences, and it is worth not confusing them with the above.

Talking loudly on public transport is a breach of manners, and so is taking a phone call on a train or bus. [source:1] Playing music loudly is a nuisance, and the guidebook asks you to make sure sound does not leak from your earphones. [source:1] Wearing a backpack on your back in a crowded carriage bumps into people and is a nuisance. [source:1]

On noise at home, the guidebook frames it as awareness rather than rule: in Japan there is a consciousness that making loud sounds or voices is a nuisance to others. [source:1] It asks you to be careful about loud conversation, parties, and television or music; to avoid doing laundry, vacuuming or showering early in the morning; and to be especially careful in apartment buildings. [source:1]

Nobody will prosecute you for a 7am shower. You may, however, lose the relationship with the neighbour you will live beside for two years.

Rubbish: the part that costs money

Sorting is the famous part. The part that surprises people is that some categories are not free to throw away.

The basics first. You must observe the place and the day of the week for each type of rubbish, and follow the rules of the municipality you live in. [source:1] Generally, rubbish is put out on the morning of the day it is collected. [source:1] If you put out a type other than the one scheduled, or put it somewhere other than the designated place, it will not be collected. [source:1] And depending on your municipality, you may have to use paid bags that the municipality designates. [source:1]

Then the categories that carry charges.

Oversized rubbish — furniture such as tables and chairs, bicycles, futons — may cost money to dispose of or recycle. [source:1]

Appliance rubbish — air conditioners, televisions, refrigerators and freezers, washing machines and clothes dryers — requires you to pay a recycling fee and a collection and transport fee when you replace or discard it. [source:1] You must also use an operator licensed for collection and transport. [source:1] Where to pay and who takes the old item depends on whether you are replacing it or only discarding it: if replacing, the shop where you buy the new one; if only discarding, the shop where you bought the old one. [source:1] If you do not know which shop that was, ask your municipality. [source:1]

Read the oversized list again and note what is on it: a futon and a bicycle. Those are the two things a departing student is most likely to own and least likely to have budgeted to get rid of. Plan the end of your stay around that, not the week of your flight.

One kitchen item worth its own line: do not pour cooking oil down the sink. [source:1] Absorb it with a paper towel in the pan or solidify it with a coagulant, and dispose of it according to your municipality's rules. [source:1]

Housing: what the guidebook says you can actually apply for

The chapter on housing contains something most student guides omit, which is that private rental is not your only option.

UR rental housing is managed by the Urban Renaissance Agency. Requirements include income exceeding a standard monthly figure that UR sets. [source:1] For foreign nationals, those who need to reside continuously and who hold diplomatic or official status, special permanent residency, or mid-to-long-term resident status including permanent residents, may move in. [source:1]

A student with student residence status is a mid-to-long-term resident. So the category is open to you in principle, and the real barrier is the income requirement rather than your status. Worth asking about, because it is a different kind of tenancy from the private market.

Public housing is provided by local governments at low rent for low-income people who have difficulty with housing, with occupancy requirements including income standards set by each prefecture or municipality. [source:1] For foreign nationals, in addition to the normal requirements, there may be conditions such as having a residence status or residence record of 1 year or more. [source:1] Applications go to the prefecture or municipality managing the housing. [source:1]

For private rental housing, the guidebook's warning is short and correct: contract terms vary by property, so sufficient confirmation is necessary. [source:1]

And it points to two documents produced for foreign nationals looking for private rentals, a room-search guidebook and a guide to moving into rental housing. [source:1] The room-search guidebook covers how to search and the contract flow, the documents and costs required, move-in procedures, the rules for living in Japanese housing, move-out procedures, and the property terminology worth knowing. [source:1] It is published in a range of languages. [source:1]

That is the document to read before you sign anything, and it is free.

Toilets, briefly

Use the paper provided, and flush used paper. [source:1] The guidebook addresses this directly because in some countries used paper goes in a bin, and it notes that if you use the paper provided, blockages in a Japanese flush toilet are rare. [source:1] In department stores and stations there are many buttons, and the flush button is usually marked FLUSH. [source:1]

The short version

  • Rubbish in the wrong place can be a criminal matter, not a building-management matter. [source:1]
  • Your phone in your hand on a bicycle is illegal. [source:1]
  • Train etiquette is etiquette. Treat it seriously for the sake of living well, not because of a penalty.
  • Find out your municipality's collection days and whether it requires paid bags, in your first week. [source:1]
  • Before you leave Japan, budget and schedule disposal of your futon and bicycle. [source:1]
  • If you are renting privately, read the room-search guidebook before signing. [source:1]

Related: the chapter structure of the guidebook and how to get the current edition, in the official guidebook; the cycling rules in detail, in bicycles and traffic; what to do in an emergency, in emergency numbers; and the dormitory-versus-apartment decision that precedes all of this, in dormitory or apartment.

Everything above is from the guidebook, linked below, and municipal rules vary by municipality — yours is the authority on its own collection days and bags.

claims_without_sources: 「自転車での携帯操作が留学生を最も多く捕まえる」—— 当方の推測であり、違反件数の統計に基づくものではない。冊子が述べているのは法律で禁止されているという事実のみ。
「朝7時のシャワーで訴追されることはない」—— 条文を確認したわけではなく、冊子がマナーの項に置いていることからの読み。刑罰の有無を断定する書き方は避けた。
「ふとんと自転車は帰国時に最も処分に困る持ち物である」—— 当方の観察。冊子は粗大ごみの例として挙げているだけで、留学生との関係は述べていない。
UR 賃貸の基準月収額の具体額 —— 冊子は「ＵＲが定める基準月収額」と書くのみで金額を示していない。したがって金額を書いていない。
「UR は留学生にとって民間とは違う種類の賃貸である（保証人の扱いなど）」—— 制度の詳細は冊子に書かれていないため、本文では「違う種類の賃貸」と述べるに留め、保証人について具体的に書いていない。
公営住宅の「1年以上」という要件 —— 冊子の記述どおりだが、出典が約14万字の冊子であるため、闸门はこの数字をページ上に在るという次級証拠でしか扱えない。警告が出るのが正しい状態。
部屋探しのガイドブックの言語数 —— 冊子は言語ごとのリンクを列挙しているが、総数を数字で示していない。自分で数えて断定することは避け「a range of languages」と書いた。
